lesson.title: Why We Need a Shorthand: Summation Notation
lesson.summary: Riemann sums add up dozens, hundreds, or thousands of terms, and summation notation is the compact language mathematicians developed so those long sums do not have to be written out term by term.
lesson.body:
Look back at the left Riemann sum computed a couple of chapters ago: Δx times [f(x0) + f(x1) + f(x2) + f(x3)]. With only four terms, writing every one of them out by hand is no trouble at all. But a Riemann sum with n = 4 is a toy example built for hand computation. Real approximations often use n = 100, n = 1000, or far more subintervals to get close to the exact integral, and nobody is going to write out f(x0) + f(x1) + f(x2) plus all the way through f(x99) term by term, let alone a thousand terms. Summation notation exists to solve exactly this problem: it lets you describe a long, structured sum in one compact line, no matter how many terms it actually contains.

The core idea of summation notation is that most of the sums you care about in calculus are not random collections of numbers, they are generated by a single pattern applied over and over with one changing input. In a Riemann sum, that pattern is take f at some sample point and multiply by Δx, and the changing input is which subinterval you are on. Once you can describe the pattern and the range over which it repeats, you have described the entire sum, no matter how many terms it expands to.

Consider the sum of the first four perfect squares: 1² + 2² + 3² + 4². Written out longhand like that, it is easy enough to compute directly: 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30. Now imagine the same pattern extended to the first fifty perfect squares, 1² + 2² + 3² and so on through 50². The pattern, square the term, and the range, 1 through 50, are both simple to state in words, but writing all fifty terms out longhand would be tedious and error prone. This is precisely the gap a compact notation needs to fill: a way to write add up i squared as i runs from 1 to 50 without writing fifty separate terms.

This is exactly the situation a Riemann sum puts you in. The formula from the Riemann sum chapter, add up f(x_i*) times Δx for every subinterval, is a pattern, multiply a function value by Δx, applied across a range, i = 1 through n. Summation notation is the tool that lets that formula be written precisely and compactly regardless of whether n is 4 or 4000. The next chapter introduces the actual symbol, the capital Greek letter sigma, that makes this compact form possible.
